item.title: The 10 Chase Cards Everybody Wants from Mastery Pack: Assassin
item.description:
Flesh and Blood|collecting|finance

The 10 Chase Cards Everybody Wants from Mastery Pack: Assassin

Don't let powerful cards sneak up on you! Flesh and Blood's latest Mastery Pack is stuffed with must-have cards.

By Scott Mines

|@HowlingMines
|

Published Nov 13, 2026

|

8 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: The Cards Everybody Wants

Guys, gals and non-binary pals: the doctor is in.  

Even better, he's not the only one. Mastery Pack: Assassin is the latest instalment of Flesh and Blood's increasingly popular ancillary booster sets, designed to provide everything that fans of the Assassin class will need to get into the class, upgrade their decks and inflict crippling diseases on their opponent. 

It might just be the most important Mastery Pack so far. Mastery Pack: Assassin not only revitalizes neglected heroes like Uzuri, Switchblade and Arakni, Huntsman, but introduces the horrific Dr.Mortimer, Blight of the Pits into the Classic Constructed format. It's also the foundation for Outbreak, the first booster set of 2027. That's some awfully big boots to fill...

...and don't worry. I'll have an Armory Deck upgrade guide for Dr. Mortimer, Blight of the Pits for you next week. I'm in the kitchen myself, hang tight for a minute.

Somehow, Mastery Pack: Assassin has a little something for everyone despite clearly being tailored towards fans of the stabby stabby. If you're already deeply intrenched in the class, you're obviously covered — but there's also timely reprints for players entering the class for the first time and a handful of generics that'll fit into any collection. That's to say nothing of the high-end marvel collectibles. There's something for everyone in here!

So, what should you be hoping to find when you pop open those packs in the coming days? I'm glad you asked, mysterious voice on the internet. Here's some of my top picks for the most coveted cards from Flesh and Blood's Mastery Pack: Assassin. 

#10: Outbreak

You are not high enough on this card. There. I said it.  

Outbreak is the kind of card that's obviously powerful, but it's difficult to grasp how ubiquitous it has the potential to be until you've got a couple of games in. It's the golden rule in Flesh and Blood: "Blue block-threes that you actually want to play sometimes are kind of busted"

I think Outbreak is clearly at its best in Dr Mortimer, who can cure one of the ineffectual diseases to generate Silver, but a reaction that'll be worth upwards of five points of value that's so easily pitch stacked is appealing to any assassin. Taking all the tempo from your opponent with on-hits also lends itself towards cards that allow you to convert your full hand, which is exactly what Outbreak will allow you to do. 

#9: Banger!

You can't call a card Banger! and not design it as a certified banger.  

This card is horrific in the endgame when life totals begin to plummet, but it's also potentially quite strong as a blue that Uzuri, Switchblade is interested in switching in. If the opponent underblocks? Great, you're hitting for seven. If they overblock? Just leave your small attack on the chain and cash Banger! in for a Silver.

I'm also in love with the idea of pitch stacking a copy of this card next to a couple of Just a Nick, or sleeving it up in Kayo, Underhanded Cheat as a sweet target for your hero ability. It's so difficult to end up with a positive exchange for the opponent regardless of if they block or not.

I'm expecting Banger! to be a solid role player in several decks, so I'd suggest snapping up some copies while you can.  

#8: Remember the Mists

I feel similar ways about Remember the Mists as I do about Outbreak. While it's clearly at its best in a particular assassin, it's probably good enough to see universal play as a flexible blue with upside.  

Remember the Mists is Surgical Extraction at home. While you can't always rip away a meaningful card from the opposing hand, you can seriously mess with arrows and blue cards that the opponent intended to pitch away to fuel their turn. If you're really lucky, you'll find a pesky fabled gem in their hand and send it into the abyss forever.  

Despite the obvious power in Uzuri, I think Remember the Mists is also a meaningful upgrade to Arakni, Huntsman. The deck typically relies on Surgical Extraction to remove the final cards from the hand of an opponent that you're trying to fatigue. Remember the Mists provides another three blues that achieve the same thing, which is a pretty big boon in my book.  

#7: Expense Not Spared 

This card reads like Swordmaster's Shine just chugged an energy drink, but I actually think it's entirely fine at time of writing. Silver is a finite resource for many of these heroes and should be seen as a real cost to play Expense Not Spared.

Think about it this way: the floor for two silver is rebuying a Graven Gloves (or similar piece in a different slot), so we should consider two Silver to be worth at least two value. If you squint, that makes Expense Not Spared more of a +3 than a +5. That's still quite good, but it makes those comparisons to other cards a little misleading.  

The power of this card will come in forcing through on-hits. The best possible fork is having Dr.Mortimer, Blight of the Pits active as you attack to convince your opponent that you're looking for Go Again, then whacking them over the head with five damage at reaction speed instead.

#6: Important Assassin Reprints

I'm going to cobble a few of these together into one entry, so they don't eat up my entire list. The fact I need to consider doing that is a good sign for the health of Mastery Pack: Assassin.   

It's no secret that several of the staple assassin threats were getting a little expensive as the hype for Mastery Pack: Assassin and Outbreak began to swell. While this product didn't quite manage to tackle all those price increases (it was never going to), it does contain many important ones for players getting into Assassin.  

Persuasive Prognosis, Pain in the Backside and Blacktek Whisperers are staples of the class and should be cheaper than they have been in a long time in the immediate wake of release. There's no better time to purchase them if you've been sitting on your hands. 

#5: Phial of Calamity

It takes a really potent piece of kit to usurp a dagger, but I think Phial of Calamity has such a terrifying threat of activation is specific matchups that the juice will be worth the squeeze.  

In aggressive matchups where the opponent doesn't want to block, this says "if you ignore my dagger, your arsenal is gone". In Assassin/Ranger matchups, on-demand Frailty is both your best friend and fuels half the cost to get Phail of Calamity back into play. It also causes headaches once your opponent is sitting at three life because of Bloodrot Pox.  

In Arakni, 5L!p3d 7hRu 73h cR4X, I think this card is kind of heinous. Kiss of Death gets to double dip on whatever affliction you decided to afflict thanks to Flick Knives.  If you do that multiple times in a game? Disgusting. 

#4: Silver (Marvel)

Despite being the least flashy card on this list, the marvel variant of the Silver token is very flashy in real life. That's exactly why everybody is going to want it.  

Silver is slowly becoming an important part of every assassin's toolkit, and most Flesh and Blood players are magpies. If my deck makes Silver, I need the nice one or I'm a disgrace to my class. It really is as simple as that.  

#3: Cadaver Handlers

I'm down for you to quote me on this one. Cadaver Handlers are not only the best card in Mastery Pack: Assassin: they're one of the top five equipment ever printed.  

This thing is NUTS. It's never been more difficult to block a Codex of Frailty into a Leave No Witnesses. Cadaver Handlers effects the whole chain link for some reason, so even if you hold your defense reaction until after it's been activated, it'll still get shrunk.

Thankfully, that does mean that it won't break Temper equipment that hadn't blocked before, but that seems like a small reprieve. I bought a cold foil yesterday because I believe this card is stupid. I really can't think a better endorsement than that.  

#2: Dr. Mortimer, Blight of the Pits (Marvel)

In the era of FaB 3.0, I get the feeling that adult hero marvels are going to become a hot commodity. Frankly, they already were. Have you seen the price on Viserai, the Forsaken lately?!  

The vibe on Dr.Mortimer, Blight of the Pits heading into release is pretty darn good. There are high expectations for the hero straight out of the gate and an army of fans who love the Assassin class. I'm expecting the premium version of his adult hero card to become a small goldmine if he lives up to his potential.  

It shouldn't hit the highs of the Jarl Vetreidi marvel, but frankly it doesn't need to. 

#1: Dynasty Attack Marvels

But these might. What an absurd introduction to FAB 3.0!

Leave No Witnesses and Surgical Extraction have been a core part of Assassin's identity since the class first released back in Dynasty, while Eradicate has seen a strong amount of play for the weakest card in the cycle. This trio is assassin. It makes so much sense to give them the premium treatment as the headliner for this set. 

These are all going to be grails for collectors and players alike, but I'm expecting Leave No Witnesses to be in a league of its own. It's been a three of in every Assassin deck since it was printed, so those serious assassin players are going to see it as an incredibly worthwhile investment.

item.title: Have Grand Master Rares in Yu-Gi-Oh Kept Their Value?
item.description:
Yu-Gi-Oh!|finance

Have Grand Master Rares in Yu-Gi-Oh Kept Their Value?

Do the rares just keep getting rarer?

By Ken Nishi

|

Published Nov 17, 2026

|

6 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Grand Master Rares were one of the biggest additions to the Yu-Gi-Oh TCG in 2026, generating tons of excitement when they were first introduced in Magnificent Monsters. With their distinctive hieroglyphic borders, beautiful foiling and extremely limited availability, these serialized cards quickly established themselves as some of the most desirable collectibles in the game. Unsurprisingly, that excitement translated into some pretty impressive price tags, with many confirmed sales in the four-figure and, in some cases, even five-figure prices.

However, a lot can change in a few months, especially when it comes to the secondary market. Now that the initial excitement has had some time to settle, it's worth taking another look at these cards to see how they've performed. Have Grand Master Rares managed to maintain their impressive prices, or has some of that initial hype started to fade? Let's take a look at how the market has changed and whether these exclusive cards have managed to hold their value.

What Makes Grand Master Rares So Desirable?

Grand Master Rares actually made their debut in the OCG before eventually making their way overseas to the TCG. Their introduction in Japan generated considerable interest among collectors, and that excitement carried over when the rarity was finally announced for Europe and the Americas. The original wave contained 18 different cards, featuring retrained versions of some of the most iconic monsters from across the Yu-Gi-Oh! anime series.

Part of what makes Grand Master Rares so interesting is that they aren't all equally desirable. While every card shares the same limited print run, certain monsters naturally have much more appeal to a wider range of collectors. Iconic monsters like Dark Magician and Stardust Dragon have considerable nostalgic appeal, while others might attract buyers primarily because of their artwork or personal significance. At the same time, specific numbers, such as 1/100 or 100/100, might command a premium compared to other numbers. As we'll see, those differences in demand have played an important role in how individual Grand Master Rares have performed on the secondary market.

What Has Happened to the Price of Grand Master Rares?

Of course, it's impossible to look at the "market price" of any individual Grand Master Rare; each card is unique, so the differences that we noted above can significantly influence what they've sold for, especially given that the cards are only a couple of months old. That said, we can try to get a better idea of how the market has changed by comparing sales from September with more recent transactions.

We'll start with Dark Magical Curtain, a new Spell card featuring Dark Magician Girl that many players are expecting to be the most valuable Grand Master Rare from the set. Looking back at September, we saw several copies move on eBay at $28,000, $36,000 and $39,000. These prices were considerably higher than some of the sales we had seen for Japanese Grand Master Rares after their initial hype had settled down. In fact, one Japanese copy sold in late August for about $15,000. After those early sales, however, it does seem that the market has cooled off considerably; earlier this month, we saw another English Grand Master Rare sell at a similar price point of $15,600. This latest sale suggests that a lot of the initial hype surrounding Grand Master Rares has started to cool off, with buyers less willing to pay the premium prices we saw when the set first dropped. 

However, the current listings tell a different story. For duelists that might be looking to pick up a Grand Master Rare Dark Magical Curtain, the cheapest copy currently available on eBay has an asking price of $46,290! Of course, this doesn't mean that the card is going to sell at that price, but it's a significant gap in price from the most recent sold listing. Moving forward, it'll be interesting to see whether supply or demand becomes a bigger driving force behind the card's price. We could see sellers feel pressured to move the card and accept lower offers, or we could see buyers believe that the card has long-term growth potential and look to meet sellers at their asking prices.

In contrast, let's consider a card like Gagaga Magician - Gagaga Magic! Although Gagaga Magician is a card that most duelists are familiar with, it's not the same household name that cards like Dark Magician and Stardust Dragon are. However, it's still available as a Grand Master Rare, and a Grand Master Rare copy of Gagaga Magician - Gagaga Magic is just as difficult to pull as any of the others! That said, back in September, we did see a Grand Master Rare Gagaga Magician sell for about $3,500. Since then, we've actually seen some sales that suggest the price hasn't moved too much; we just saw one sell for $3,300 at the beginning of November. Although two copies did sell for about $2,200 and $1,500, they were each PSA 9 copies, which suggests there may be some condition or card quality issues responsible for bringing the prices down slightly.

With Gagaga Magician, there are currently a few listed on eBay, but the cheapest ones are still sitting at about $3,000 each. Even though Gagaga Magician isn't a particularly popular monster, its relatively stable sales suggest that there's still considerable demand for Grand Master Rares beyond the most recognizable names. With such limited supply, sellers also have little incentive to accept offers they consider too low.

Ultimately, these two cards really demonstrate how different the market looks for different Grand Master Rares. While some cards haven't lived up to the early hype prices from when Magnificent Monsters first dropped, others have retained value well. Either way, it's worth remembering that there's an incredibly limited supply of these cards on the market, and even just a couple of transactions could significantly influence how we perceive these cards and their valuations. At the moment, it's still difficult to say for sure whether the market is beginning to stabilize, or if there's plenty of movement ahead.

What Does the Future Hold for Grand Master Rares?

There are still plenty of factors that could influence the prices of Grand Master Rares moving forward. The second wave of Grand Master Rares in Magnificent Maestros, as well as any other Grand Master Rares that we receive in future sets, could certainly shift market attention in any number of directions. A cool new card for a nostalgic theme could reinvigorate interest from older players and push them to take an interest in collecting again. Meanwhile, future support for certain themes could bring renewed attention to existing cards that might otherwise fly under the radar. Broader trends in the market will also play a role, as demand for premium Yu-Gi-Oh cards in general can shift alongside changes in the overall card landscape. There's simply no way to know exactly where these cards will end up with so many variables still in play.

Despite some initial price declines, it's important to remember that Grand Master Rares are still relatively new, and we're only a few months removed from their debut in the TCG. There's plenty of room for these cards to establish themselves as high-end pieces alongside One Piece's Manga Rares and Riftbound's Signature Overnumbered cards, but that kind of reputation doesn't happen overnight. If there's one thing we've learned from the collectibles market, it's that time can make all the difference. We'll have to check back in a few years to see whether Grand Master Rares have managed to stand the test of time.

item.title: CookieRunWarp Time With Shadow Milk Cookie and ST11 - Timeline of Fate
item.description:
CookieRun|casual

Warp Time With Shadow Milk Cookie and ST11 - Timeline of Fate

Craft your perfect timeline with this new CookieRun: Braverse TCG starter deck.

By Drew Knapp

|@FenrirRex
|

Published Nov 17, 2026

|

3 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

I am the champion of preconstructed deck play. I live for an out-of-the-box experience, and a game will always sell me immediately if it can give me something that's great the moment you crack it open and start jamming games. CookieRun: Braverse TCG has consistently been exactly that already, and you can find my rankings of the previous starter decks below.

The good news is that you are now not limited to those 10 starters, as we've just gotten a new one added to the roster: ST11 - Timeline of Fate. I need to get in a few more rounds with the deck, so I won't immediately say that it now tops the list, however it's performing very well and has some powerful synergy right from the start. If we were to travel to the future, I wouldn't be surprised if this moved all the way up to the best precon currently on the shelves

A Wonderfully Warped List

Cookies:

  • 4 Wizard Cookie
  • 4 Marble Bread Cookie
  • 4 Mochaccino Cookie
  • 4 Black Sapphire Cookie
  • 4 String Gummy Cookie
  • 4 Espresso Cookie
  • 4 Candy Apple Cookie
  • 2 Pain de Campagne Cookie
  • 2 Ash Salt Cookie
  • 2 Croissant Cookie
  • 4 Parfait Cookie

Trap:

  • 4 Unending Play
  • 2 Corrupted Seal Tree
  • 4 Destruction of a Pastless Future

Stage:

  • 4 Warped Timeline

Item:

  • 2 Whispering Study Hall
  • 2 Milky Star of the Final Act
  • 4 Time Manipulator

Extra Deck:

  • 2 Shadow Milk Cookie

The deck has an extremely powerful core right up front. The deck is designed wonderfully to find Warped Timeline, play a nearly unstoppable Shadow Milk Cookie alongside it, and then use cards like Croissant Cookie to make sure that the game plan continues until you achieve victory. The deck is very good at working through its entire hand to gain consistent access to Croissant Cookie's bonus damage.

Black Sapphire Cookie, Pain de Campagne Cookie, and Ash Salt Cookie all continue to show off the core strategy of the deck. You get some impressive bonuses by leaning into Shadow Milk Cookie, can keep Warped Timeline on the board quite painlessly with the help of Pain de Campagne Cookie, and Ash Salt Cookie once again takes advantage of your dwindling hand size.

Finally, I have to highlight some of the delicious support that is helping your core deck pop off. Unending PLay and Candy Apple Cookie both help take away options from your opponent's hand and keep the defensive game going, while Milky Star of the Final Act keeps the damage flowing into the end game. Combined, the total kit of this deck is exceptional.

Looking to the Future

The deck itself does, as I've said, play wonderfully right out of the box. However, I understand that many players don't just want the preconstructed experience. No, you want to instead use this as a jumping off point for your next legit deck. Well, I have good news! It's quite easy to upgrade the core of this deck, and in fact I don't think it even needs all that much to become functionally competitive.

The first option, and honestly the next step, is just to buy a second copy of the deck. This way you can run the max 4-of copies of all the 2-of cards that start in the list. At time of writing it might be cheaper to just fill those slots with singles, but that's not common with a lot of starter product– you'll almost certainly be safe to just nab that second copy, max out all the best cards, and start rocking the deck.

Otherwise, there are a few staples that I might recommend, but the deck comes packed with what I would essentially call side grades to those staples anyway. Meaning, you don't actually need to go out of your way to get them. Instead, I would strongly consider adding on extra Shadow Milk Cookie synergies by filling out your deck (and your extra deck!) with your favorite versions of Shadow Milk Cookie.

You'll notice that Shadow Milk Cookie is very good at getting up to shenanigans with your extra deck, and you can very freely pack those slots with alternate reality versions of him (very fitting for this deck I might add) and get a proper little toolkit of abilities. After that, you'll have something that should be able to play perfectly at your locals.

item.title: Off-Meta Minute: Amber Amethyst Merida
item.description:
Disney Lorcana|competitive

Off-Meta Minute: Amber Amethyst Merida

Muuuuuum! It's just my bow!

By Scott Mines

|@HowlingMines
|

Published Nov 18, 2026

|

4 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Deck diversity has always been an appealing part of card games for me. As a competitor, I tend to prefer narrower metagames that are easier for me to target, but as a person? Let me turn up to my weekly event and play against every different flavor of nonsense out there. I wanna see what kind of brew gets you out of bed in the morning.

That's a big part of why I started Off-Meta Minute here on TCGplayer. If you cook up something cool, you deserve your flowers. Somehow, I have the platform to give them to you while also encouraging up-and-coming Illumineers to give your madness a shot. It's one of the coolest parts of my job.

Sometimes it's difficult to give the right person flowers, though. Sometimes, a sweet archetype pops up, and I cannot quite place where it originally came from as it lights up the tournament tables like wildfire.

That's what happened with Amber Amethyst Merida.

ELJ_GHartuck's Amber Amethyst Merida - 186th Place at Disney Lorcana Challenge Villain Challenge: Gaston 

I'd also like to mention Liam Dolecki's Top 256 performance with this archetype in DLC London's Main Event 1. The deck clearly has competitive legs; I just like GHartuck's list a little better.

This deck is a side grade to the more popular variants of Amber Amethyst with a few cute tricks baked in. We'll start with the namesake card, Merida - Wisp Conjurer.

 

We don't get Merlin - Rabbit or Genie - Wish Fulfilled anymore, but you can still accelerate into a pair of four-cost Amethyst characters that can draw you cards. You can lean on Mickey Mouse - Best in Town or Hamm - Piggy Bank within your first two turns to curve cleanly into a copy of Merlin - Profoundly Curious (who refunds you for the help) or a difficult-to-contest Merida - Wisp Conjurer that immediately draws a card and threatens to snowball out of control.

 

The best follow-up to Merida is often just a second copy, who can enter play exerted to draw you two cards in tandem with her counterpart. That's not enough to build a deck around though, so you'll need to rely on some other friends to help maximize the number of cards you can score from Merida. How do you do that? Bodyguard.

Rex - Protective Dinosaur is the best cheap bodyguard in this ink combination, regularly trading up for bigger characters and scoring you some lore in the process. Lionheart - Incumbent Mayor is an absolute tank with impossibly difficult stats to push through. Both will gain you incidental lore while banking cards of Merida, leading to an opponent who is frantically trying to bust through the wall to stop the card advantage while falling further and further behind.

But my favorite piece of spice? Remember Me. In those long, grindy games, it's not uncommon for an opponent to think they're running you out of cards before a Merida and a Hamm sing this backbreaking song, allowing you to play like three characters from your discard exerted and draw a card off every single one. You don't want to draw too many of these, so I like having only a single copy — but it's an army in a can all by itself.

 

I alluded to it briefly when talking about Rex and Lionheart, but this deck can close the door shockingly fast once those cards get spinning. Merlin's Shop and Smithy - Magical Market is an annoyingly sticky location that you can ferry your characters to for some extra lore and card draw. Even better, nobody wants to waste their time removing it. Once you enter the late game with a bucket of leftover ink drops, sometimes it'll just be sitting there waiting to win the game. It's a snazzy piece of cardboard.

I also wanted to mention how well the Demona - Imperious Spellcaster package slots into this deck. Of course, the namesake variant is a beast of a card by itself. It'll happily discard one of those cards you've drawn to turn into a turbocharged Madam Mim - Fox, but it can also fill the discard for a timely Remember Me in this shell. Demona - Betrayer of the Clan is also a phenomenal character to accelerate into with Hamm - Piggy Bank against aggressive decks and loves to be juiced up with Rush.

But the high roll? Use Demona - Scourge of the Wyvern Clan to lock down the opposing board before the Imperious Spellcaster sends her rushing into battle. I've had a handful of games where I've been able to play both of these cards with Remember Me and proceeded to blast my opponent's board to bits. It's very sweet.

Closing Thoughts 

I'm very glad that the Hyperia City metagame continues to offer some room to breathe for players who aren't enamored with Amber Emerald or Emerald Steel. Merida - Wisp Conjurer is an absurdly sweet card that didn't really get any time in the sun when it was released back in Attack of the Vine!, so I'm overjoyed to see players cooking up deck lists that allow her to shine. Is Remember Me the sauce? I don't know for sure, but I can't help but hope.

Have further questions? Let me know over at @HowlingMines on X (formerly Twitter) or @howlingmines.com over on Bluesky! Alternatively, give my other work here on TCGplayer a peek if you'd like another slice of everything nice about your favorite game. 

But until next time. I've been HowlingMines, you've been amazing! 

Stay safe out there — and happy gaming!

item.title: MagicCon: Atlanta Gave Us A Glimpse At Nauctis, But The Big News Is The New TV Show
item.description:
Magic: The Gathering|casual|news|opinion

MagicCon: Atlanta Gave Us A Glimpse At Nauctis, But The Big News Is The New TV Show

Darling, it's better.

By Jason Coles

|

Published Nov 18, 2026

|

4 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

MagicCon Atlanta has concluded now, and you might have seen a few of our favorite colleagues there. There were plenty of exciting reveals over the weekend, including a first-look at Nauctis: The Sunken Realm. The new booster is set in a world of oceans and sea creatures, and deep beneath the surface lies a mysterious darkness. As big of a reveal as Nauctis was, I personally can't stop thinking about the upcoming Magic: The Gathering TV show Planeswalker. 

UnGoogleable 

Ignoring how absurdly hard it is to search for "MTG Planeswalker" and get within a hundred kilometers of the show itself, things are looking pretty good for us Magic fans. The showrunner for Planeswalker is Terry Matalas, who's had a solid run of things recently. Not only was he showrunner for two seasons of Star Trek: Picard, but he also worked on VisionQuest too, which is arguably one of the best Marvel series in a long time. 

Matalas will once again be working with Star Trek: Picard and VisionQuest writer Cindy Appel, as well as the production studio Digic. Digic is the studio behind a few of the Secret Level episodes on Amazon Prime and a massive catalog of video game trailers and cinematics. There's good reason to be confident–and excited–with a team this stacked. Of course, the sneak peek helps too. 

The show is going to be centering Chandra as she meets other Planeswalkers and travels through different worlds. Chandra is a natural for a protagonist of a show at this point as she's not only got the most exciting personality of the core Planeswalkers, but also possesses the flashiest skill set. Fire sells, and we all know it. I can't wait to learn more.

Under The Sea 

Nauctis: The Sunken Realm is going to be in our hands on February 5th, and it's also arriving with four Commander Decks. The set will bring with it God Packs, which are booster packs containing all rare and mythic cards for the maximum amount of hype. These will appear in both Play and Collector Boosters, but will be quite rare to open.

We haven't seen much in terms of cards here, but the previews so far have been really exciting. Calmwater Mentor is a four-mana seal monk in white that lets you find up to two creature cards with 2 power or less and put them into your hand when it enters. Not only is that an absurd ability on its own, but also makes it a lot easier to pull off all sorts of combos. Also it's a seal, and seals are adorable as we all know. 

On the other end of the size scale we're getting Salinae, the Ocean Mother an eight-mana blue 5/7 whale god with trample. Eight mana might seem like a lot, but it gets a discount on its casting cost based on your devotion to blue. This thing spits out copies of your artifacts and creatures whenever you cast them, turning the copy into a 1/1 fish. Expect to see this absolutely everywhere in Commander, and potentially as a great finisher for control decks too. 

Tecton, Malignant Ruin is another eight-mana card that can be cheaper, but this time it's based on the permanents in your graveyard. It's a 5/5 with menace and deathtouch that turns anything you sacrifice into card draw. The new Abyssal Lotus also cares about permanents in your graveyard too. It costs 0 mana, comes in tapped, and can be tapped and exiled for three mana, but only if you have eight or more permanents in your graveyard. It's a solid card, but feels pretty reigned-in when it comes to pure power. Ring of Unity is another artifact, but a seven-mana one that allows all of your artifacts to tap for two colorless mana. If you think one Sol Ring is annoying, then you'll abhor this. 

The final card was Goramou the Coral-Taken a three-mana red and green shark that makes a blood token when it enters. Do you remember blood tokens? They can be tapped and sacrificed to discard a card and draw a card. When you do discard any land cards, you can exile them and then put them into play tapped at the beginning of your next end step. The art work on each version is also absolutely horrifying in the best way. 

It's pretty clear that Nauctis: The Sunken Realm is, rather fittingly, filled with horrors and a love of putting things into your graveyard, so I'm expecting a lot of sacrificing and discarding to make an appearance alongside plenty of things to discard and sacrifice. That's on its way next year, so maybe we'll get a little Magic news break for the rest of 2026.

item.title: Crustle Deck Guide (Pokémon TCG)
item.description:
Pokémon|competitive

Crustle Deck Guide (Pokémon TCG)

*crab rave ensues*

By Natalie Millar

|@nataliem9999
|

Published Nov 18, 2026

|

4 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: Pokémon Deck Guides

Hello everyone! Crustle is one of the most disliked decks in the current format due to its stall-like game plan, but I believe that this deck can produce interesting games and is one of the few decks that can reliably win by decking out your opponent. This deck also gained a few options from Delta Reign, and I wouldn't be surprised to see if have a solid showing at the Latin America International Championships this weekend!

Crustle Deck Guide

This deck relies very heavily on Crustle's Mysterious Rock Inn ability to prevent opposing Pokémon ex from damaging it, then you attack with Superb Scissors and heal the Crustle with Jumbo Ice Cream and the new Tasty Rice Ball from Delta Reign.

This particular deck list doesn't have Energy acceleration - you just attach three times to your Crustle and attack with it. Since Crustle only gives up one Prize, you can also use Mega Kangaskhan ex's Run Errand ability to draw cards. Despite giving up three Prize cards, as long as you don't put down multiple Mega Kangaskhan in matchups where you need to use Crustle, your opponent will eventually be forced to KO a Crustle if they want to win the game. Dwebble's Ascension attack also helps you get into Crustle very quickly, as if you open Dwebble you can evolve as soon as turn one going second.

Growling Grass Energy and Hero's Cape gives your Crustle more HP to make it tougher to KO. Mist Energy prevents effects such as the residual damage from Phantom Dive, Alakazam's Powerful Hand and the confusion from Munkidori. Spiky Energy looks a little weird in this deck, but it often pushes opposing single-Prize attackers into range of a Superb Scissors. Spikey Energy can also push attackers like Dudunsparce ex which can hit through Mysterious Rock Inn into the range of two Superb Scissors.

Once the initial Mega Kangaskhan goes down, you'll struggle to draw cards, and the many supporters like Lillie's Determination, Team Rocket's Petrel and Hilda help find more cards without Run Errand. Eri and Xerosic's Machinations both pressure your opponents resources and prevents them from stacking too many important cards in their hand. Festival Grounds is to remove various Special Conditions from your Crustle, and it also removes the Poison from opposing Mega Sharpedo ex and N's Zoroark decks, preventing them from getting extra chip damage in with Binding Mochi. Lumiose City finds extra Pokémon, and Prism Tower draws extra cards. All these Stadiums do look a little useless, especially when Pokémon Center Lady fills the role of Festival Grounds, but the new Legendary Pyroduct which shuts off Mysterious Rock Inn, is a very big issue for this deck, and you usually need to bump it as soon as possible to prevent your opponent KOing too many Crustles.

Four Boss's Orders chase opposing Pokémon while they're being set up, but don't be afraid to use Boss as an Energy denial card to just force your opponent to retreat. Against some of the closer matchups such as Dragapult ex, your primary win condition is usually to run them out of resources, and using Boss to keep bringing up Drakloak is very difficult for them to overcome. The new Azurill from Delta Reign is worthing considering because you can use Bouncy Bouncy Charge early to accelerate Energy onto the Crustle, but you need to open with the Azurill to do this and Mega Kangaskhan is a very strong card to open with, which makes Azurill difficult to use.

The additional four healing cards with Tasty Rice Ball massively help any matchup where you're attacking with Mega Kangaskhan. Hide & Sneak and Slowking are two matchups where you'll often avoid using Crustle altogether as your opponent can easily hit through Mysterious Rock Inn, but you can still win these matchups by attaching to Mega Kangaskhan and using Rapid Fire Combo. Against these matchups, you can try and turn into a resource denial deck, and just outlast their attacks by putting Hero's Cape on the Kangaskhan and slowly taking knockouts with Rapid Fire Combo. You won't be doing this in every matchup, but it can be a very relevant strategy.

Crustle is a fragile strategy, and your opponent does have a lot of answers to your options. While many Alakazam decks don't have Enhanced Hammer, you do need to get a lot of well-timed Eris if they have two copies of Enhanced Hammer, and you struggle to win if they include Dedenne to recycle the Hammer and remove the Mist Energy. Dragapult ex decks can play Chi-Yu TWM or Dudunsparce ex as potential answers, and there are some matchups such as Festival Lead that you currently cannot beat. You can include Cornerstone Mask Ogerpon ex to help in this matchup but many players forego this inclusion as it significantly disrupts your overall strategy. Almost every deck has ways they can make the Crustle matchup either favored or almost impossible for them to lose, which makes submitting Crustle for a tournament always a gamble since your matchups can be so polarized.

Despite how linear the strategy can seem, Crustle still produces a lot of interesting games. These stall or control strategies have been present in almost every Standard format in the Pokémon TCG, and I wouldn't be surprised if we saw more of the crab in the future!

item.title: The 10 Most Expensive Pokémon Chase Cards in Delta Reign
item.description:
Pokémon|collecting|finance

The 10 Most Expensive Pokémon Chase Cards in Delta Reign

Everybody loves Rayquaza.

By Peter Day

|

Published Nov 10, 2026

|

6 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

With Delta Reign, the Pokémon Company International is closing out 2026 by continuing the trends we saw throughout the year.

Like Perfect Order, Chaos Rising, and Pitch Black before it, Delta Reign is a relatively small English Pokémon set based on a single Japanese expansion, with one massive headliner as the set's singular focus. This time, that headliner is Rayquaza, a fan-favorite Pokémon on a level beyond that of Zygarde, Greninja, and Darkrai.

As expected, the Special Illustration Rare (SIR) and Mega Hyper Rare (MHR) versions of the Sky-High Pokémon have soared far above everything else in Delta Reign. That doesn't mean you can write off the rest of the set, however. While the other SIRs don't have anything close to Rayquaza's name recognition, more than a few of the Illustration Rares (IRs) in Delta Reign have ascended to chase status—either because the Pokémon they feature are so iconic, or for Tomokazu Komiya reasons.

Let's take a look at some of the Illustration Rares and Special Illustration Rares that are vying to be Rayquaza's opening act. These are the most valuable Pokémon cards in Delta Reign.

#10 Groudon 111/103 (Illustration Rare)

Rayquaza may be the star of Delta Reign, but the other two members of the weather trio haven't been left out. The Continent Pokémon Groudon appears as an Illustration Rare in the set, and the Sea Basin Pokémon Kyogre cameos as the promo card that comes with Delta Reign Elite Trainer Boxes.

Ryota Murayama's blazing-hot illustration adds a third contender for the title of the best-looking full-art Groudon card ever printed, alongside Nurikabe's IR Groudon from Paradox Rift and nagimiso's Team Magma's Groudon-EX. Both of those cards have topped their respective sets' price guides in the past, so it's not surprising that this Groudon has become one of the big chase cards in Delta Reign.

#9 Mega Golisopod ex 135/103 (Special Illustration Rare)

Debuting in cardboard for the first time in Delta Reign, Mega Golisopod ex has a swanky Special Illustration Rare version by prolific Pokémon artist nagimiso, and an attack that's just as appealing. With Finishing Blow, Mega Golisopod ex can deal 220 damage for a single Energy as long as its victim has any damage counters on it already.

Is that strong enough to see play? We'll have to wait until after Dragapult retires from ruling the format to find out. In the meantime, this card's harsh purple, orange, and green color scheme ensures that it stands out.

#8 Aarune 139/103 (Special Illustration Rare)

With his ability to grab multiple Stadium cards, Aarune works great in decks that want to assemble both halves of a Legendary Stadium like Legendary Pyroduct.

That's nifty, but it's not enough to make every Aarune card valuable, as evidenced by his Ultra Rare and Uncommon versions. I also wouldn't attribute the price difference solely to this card's (admittedly adorable) artwork by Shimaris Yukichi.

As far as this card's price goes, its most significant trait is just its Special Illustration Rare (SIR) rarity, typically the most-sought after rarity in modern Pokémon sets. Pokémon fans love high rarities, and art with actual backgrounds, and SIRs check both of those boxes.

#7 Eevee 114/103 (Illustration Rare)

From Growlithe to Azurill to Sprigatito, Delta Reign has an impressive lineup of Illustration Rares featuring beloved Pokémon. But none of them compare to Eevee, the pre-evolution to everyone's favorite Pokémon. (All eight of them).

Eevee has appeared on countless valuable Pokémon cards over the years, and this Illustration Rare continues the trend. Hideki Ishikawa didn't stray too far from the standard Pokémon style guide with this card, but they showed impressive attention to detail with the dappled sunlight and the stitching on the bag.

Most importantly though, this card shows Eevee in the kind of pose that would earn any pet a devoted social media following. Cute things are cute.

#6 Mega Golurk ex 137/103 (Special Illustration Rare)

Mega Golurk is another Mega-Evolved Pokémon that's getting its TCG debut in Delta Reign after appearing in Pokémon Legends: Z-A.

Goliath's Punch comes with too many restrictions and drawbacks to make it appealing to players. Thankfully, the art is attractive enough on its own. Takeshi Nakamura chose the perfect blend of sunset colors to make Mega Golurk's high-contrast yellow-and-purple color scheme look natural, even dignified.

Golurk might not be the highest-profile Pokémon in the franchise, but everyone knows a gorgeous card when they see one.

#5 Kecleon 117/103 (Illustration Rare)

Who would even think to draw a Kecleon pole-dancing in a kaleidoscopic rain forest? Only Tomokazu Komiya.

Komiya uses colors, poses, and backgrounds that wouldn't even occur to a less creative artist. His idiosyncratic style has earned his work a lot of well-deserved attention over the years, and that attention has translated into hype for cards with his name on them—especially the most outlandish ones. No surprise that his latest Crayola fever dream has found an audience.

#4 Zinnia's Trust 140/103 (Special Illustration Rare)

Zinnia earned the respect of Pokémon fans with her determined pursuit of Rayquaza in order to save the planet in Delta Episode.

As a mysterious woman connected to a fan-favorite Pokémon, Zinnia has been an immensely popular character in the franchise, and many of the cards featuring her have been as valuable as that fact implies. Now Zinnia fans have another card to chase like the fate of the world is at stake.

#3 Raikou ex 136/103 (Mega Hyper Rare)

Rayquaza's not the only Legendary Pokémon with a Special Illustration Rare card in Delta Reign. The Thunder Pokémon Raikou also has an SIR, with a stunning illustration by Oku where Raikou appears to be riding lightning down from the mountains.

For a Legendary Gen II Pokémon, Raikou hasn't appeared in many full-art cards over the years, and arguably none of them look as dynamic as this one. Raikou deserved a glow-up like this.

#2 Mega Rayquaza ex 141/103 (Mega Hyper Rare)

Since the start of the Mega Evolution Series in late 2025, every Pokémon set has had one or two gold-colored Mega Hyper Rare cards as their capstones. These are the rarest cards in their respective sets, and while they're not usually the most valuable (fans don't love the monochromatic artwork), their scarcity alone makes them incredibly valuable.

In Delta Reign, the Pokémon that got the Mega Hyper Rare treatment was none other than Mega Rayquaza ex, the set's mascot and strongest new attacker. Obviously, the gold-tinted version of the Pokémon on all the box art was always going to be one of the biggest chase cards in the set.

Just, not the biggest.

#1 Mega Rayquaza ex 138/103 (Special Illustration Rare)

By far, the most expensive Pokémon card in Delta Reign is Special Illustration Rare Mega Rayquaza ex.

Delta Reign is Rayquaza's set, and no version of Mega Rayquaza ex has collectors more excited than the SIR. That largely comes down to the art. While the Mega Hyper Rare version feels opulent, modern Pokémon collectors tend to prefer cards with actual backgrounds that show characters as living parts of the Pokémon world, not as static mascots. And Kazuki Minami's take on Mega Rayquaza is about as far from static as you can get (though it's plenty electric, har har), showing the Sky-High Pokémon in a moment of dynamic exuberance that jolts the viewer awake.
